title: Changing Jobs & Job Loss
description: Quitting well, getting laid off, and protecting your money in between.
wolfLine: Every wolf changes territory. The smart ones carry food.

notice-period.definition: The time between telling your employer you’re leaving and your last day, usually two weeks in the US.
notice-period.example: Resigning on the 1st with your last day on the 15th.

layoff.definition: Losing your job because the company is cutting jobs, not because of anything you did.
layoff.example: A warehouse closes and 80 people are laid off.

severance.definition: Money some employers pay when they let you go, often a few weeks of pay per year worked, usually with an agreement to sign.
severance.example: Four weeks of pay in exchange for signing a release.

cobra.definition: A law that lets you keep your work health plan after leaving, usually up to 18 months, but you pay the full premium yourself.
cobra.example: Your $640 a month plan, now all paid by you.

rollover.definition: Moving retirement money from one account to another, like an old 401(k) into an IRA, without cashing it out.
rollover.example: Moving $8,000 from your old job’s 401(k) into your new job’s plan.

lessons.title: Before You Quit
lessons.summary: Line up the money before you hand in the letter.

steps.prompt: What should you have before quitting?
choices: A signed offer, or savings to cover the gap
steps.explain: Never leap without a net.

steps.prompt: Your essentials cost $2,200 a month and you expect 3 months between jobs. How much should you have saved?
What else should you check before leaving?
choices: When your health insurance ends and the new one starts
steps.explain: Gaps in health coverage are expensive.

steps.prompt: Some benefits, like health insurance, can end on your last day or at the end of that month.
steps.explain: Ask HR for the exact date.

steps.prompt: Unused vacation days when you leave…
choices: may be paid out, depending on your state and company
steps.explain: Check your state’s rules and your company policy.

steps.prompt: Put a smart job switch in order.
items: Get the new offer in writing
Check when benefits end and start
steps.explain: Secure it, check it, announce it, exit well.

lessons.title: Leaving Well
lessons.summary: Notice, final pay, and not burning bridges.

steps.context: Your [[notice period]] is the time between telling your employer you’re leaving and your last day.
steps.prompt: What’s the usual notice period in the US?
steps.explain: Two weeks is the norm.

steps.prompt: In most US states, you aren’t legally required to give notice.
steps.explain: Most jobs are “at will.” Notice is about goodwill and references, unless your contract says otherwise.

steps.prompt: What’s the best way to resign?
choices: A short, polite letter with your last day
steps.explain: Short and kind.

steps.prompt: Final paycheck: 6 days at $160 a day, plus 4 unused vacation days paid out at $160. Total before deductions?
Your boss offers more money to stay. What should you weigh?
choices: Why you wanted to leave in the first place, not just the pay
steps.explain: If money wasn’t the reason, more money won’t fix it.

steps.prompt: Leaving on good terms can matter for future references.
steps.explain: Industries are smaller than they look.

lessons.title: The Gap Between Jobs
lessons.summary: The first new paycheck can be weeks away.

steps.prompt: You start a new job on the 1st. When might your first paycheck arrive?
steps.explain: Payroll runs on its own schedule.

steps.prompt: Your last paycheck lands Mar 15. Your new job starts Apr 1 and first pays Apr 19. How many days with no income?
steps.explain: 16 days left in March plus 19 days in April = 35 days.

steps.prompt: Your essentials cost about $70 a day. What does that gap cost?
What’s the best way to cover it?
steps.explain: Plan the gap before you jump.

steps.prompt: Your new job’s benefits may have a waiting period before they start.
steps.explain: Some start on day one, some after 30 or 60 days.

steps.prompt: During the gap, which costs do you cut first?
steps.explain: Wants pause. Needs don’t.

lessons.title: Laid Off: The First Week
lessons.summary: What to do, in what order.

steps.context: A [[layoff]] means losing your job because the company is cutting jobs, not because of anything you did.
steps.prompt: Laid off vs. fired: what’s the difference?
choices: A layoff is about the company. Firing is about your performance or conduct
steps.explain: Being laid off says nothing bad about you.

steps.prompt: Laid off. Put the first week in order.
items: Get everything in writing: last day, final pay, severance, benefits
steps.explain: Facts, benefits, budget, search.

steps.prompt: Apply for unemployment right away, not after your savings run out.
steps.explain: Waiting can cost you weeks of benefits.

steps.prompt: Your emergency fund is $6,000 and essentials cost $2,000 a month. How many months does it cover?
What should you not do in week one?
steps.explain: Cashing out costs taxes plus a penalty. More on that soon.

steps.prompt: Being laid off says nothing bad about your skills.
steps.explain: Companies cut jobs, not people’s worth.

lessons.title: Reading a Severance Offer
lessons.summary: What you get, and what you give up by signing.

steps.context: [[Severance]] is money some employers pay when they let you go, often a few weeks of pay per year worked. It usually comes with an agreement to sign.

doc.title: Northwind Logistics
doc.subtitle: Severance agreement
doc.note: By signing, you agree not to sue the company over your employment.

steps.prompt: How much cash does this offer include, before taxes?

doc.title: Northwind Logistics
doc.subtitle: Severance agreement
doc.note: By signing, you agree not to sue the company over your employment.

steps.prompt: What do you give up by signing?
choices: The right to sue the company over your job
steps.explain: Read the note at the bottom. That’s the trade.

steps.prompt: You can ask for more time to read a severance agreement, or have a lawyer look at it.
steps.explain: Never sign something big on the spot.

steps.prompt: Severance pay is…
steps.explain: It shows up on your W-2.

steps.prompt: 4 weeks of severance on a $52,000 salary. How much?
What’s the best use of severance?
choices: Covering essentials while you job hunt
steps.explain: It’s a bridge, not a bonus.

lessons.title: Keeping Health Insurance
lessons.summary: Two ways to stay covered between jobs.

steps.context: [[COBRA]] lets you keep your work health plan after you leave, usually for up to 18 months, but you pay the whole premium yourself, plus a small fee.
steps.prompt: What’s the catch with COBRA?
choices: You pay the full premium your employer used to share
steps.explain: Same plan, much bigger bill.

lines.label: Monthly premium, same plan as before

docs.title: Marketplace plan
docs.subtitle: HealthCare.gov
docs.note: New plan. Check your doctors are covered.

steps.prompt: Which costs less per month?

lines.label: Monthly premium, same plan as before

docs.title: Marketplace plan
docs.subtitle: HealthCare.gov
docs.note: New plan. Check your doctors are covered.

steps.prompt: Over 3 months, how much does the Marketplace plan save?
Losing job-based coverage lets you sign up on the Marketplace outside the usual enrollment window.
steps.explain: You usually have 60 days to pick a plan.

steps.prompt: When might COBRA make sense anyway?
choices: When you’re mid-treatment with doctors you need to keep
steps.explain: Sometimes keeping your doctors is worth the price.

steps.prompt: Going without health insurance between jobs is a smart way to save.
steps.explain: One emergency can cost more than years of premiums.

steps.context: When you leave a job, your 401(k) stays yours. You can usually leave it, move it to your new job’s plan, or do a [[rollover]] into an IRA, an account you open yourself.
steps.prompt: What’s a rollover?
choices: Moving retirement money to another retirement account
steps.explain: The money stays invested and untaxed.

steps.prompt: Cashing out a 401(k) before age 59½ usually means income tax plus a 10% penalty.
steps.explain: And the money stops growing.

steps.prompt: You cash out $10,000. What’s the 10% penalty?
Add about 22% income tax. What do the tax and penalty come to together?
What’s left of the $10,000?
What’s usually the best move with an old 401(k)?
choices: Roll it into your new plan or an IRA
Cash it out for a trip
steps.explain: Keep it growing, tax-free, for future you.

lessons.title: Theo Gets Laid Off
lessons.summary: Severance, savings and unemployment: how far do they stretch?

story.title: The warehouse closes
story.body:
Theo was laid off on Friday when his warehouse closed. He got **$6,600** in severance after taxes and has **$5,400** in his emergency fund.

His bare-bones costs (rent, food, car, phone, utilities) are **$2,400** a month. He’s approved for unemployment of about **$1,800** a month, which in his state lasts up to **6** months.

steps.prompt: Severance plus emergency fund: how much does Theo have?
Unemployment covers $1,800 of his $2,400 a month. How much must come from savings each month?
After 6 months of unemployment, how much savings is left?
After that, savings cover the full $2,400. How many more full months? Round down.
What’s Theo’s smartest move this week?
choices: Apply for jobs and keep the budget bare-bones
steps.explain: About 9 months of runway. Use it well.

steps.prompt: Theo’s emergency fund turned a crisis into a hard but manageable stretch.
steps.explain: That’s exactly what it was for.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

Why does COBRA usually cost so much more than your old paycheck deduction?
choices: Your employer no longer pays its share of the premium
steps.explain: Same plan, full price.

steps.prompt: In most states, the law requires you to give two weeks’ notice.
steps.explain: It’s a custom, not a law, in most states.
